title: Watching One Channel Open and Shut

scenes.tts: Membrane current measured across a whole cell was thought to be the sum of many small pores opening and closing. The steps of one pore were too small to see against the noise of a large membrane. One open channel passes a few picoamps, a few trillionths of an amp. Until single-channel recording, what one channel does had to be inferred from thousands acting at once.
scenes.visual: A membrane strip of many small channels and the jagged whole-cell trace they sum to; one channel's tiny step sits hidden in noise next to a question mark; the many channels fade to one marked with a question.

scenes.tts: A glass pipette, with a tip about a micrometre across, is pressed against a cell and sealed to the membrane with slight suction. The seal must resist above a gigohm, so current flows through the patch and not around the rim. Neher and Sakmann's earliest seals were about ten to twenty megohms, and leak around the rim buried the signal in noise. The 1981 paper describes seals of a billion to a hundred billion ohms, called giga seals.
scenes.visual: Pipette lowers onto the membrane; current path through the patch versus leak under the rim; resistance readout drops to megohms with a noisy trace, then jumps on suction to gigaohm range with a clean trace.
scenes.caption: A glass pipette, with a tip about a micrometre across, is pressed against a cell and sealed to the membrane with slight suction. The seal must resist above a gigohm, so current flows through the patch and not around the rim. Neher and Sakmann's earliest seals were about 10 to 20 megohms, and leak around the rim buried the signal in noise. The 1981 paper describes seals of 10⁹ to 10¹¹ ohms, called giga-seals.

scenes.tts: An amplifier holds the pipette at a voltage you choose and records the current that flows. That is voltage clamp. In the cell-attached form, the patch stays on the cell. With an agonist in the pipette, one channel's openings appear as square steps. Pull the patch off with its cytoplasmic face exposed to the bath, and you have an inside-out patch. You can change the solution on that face. Start from whole-cell mode and pull away instead, and the membrane reseals with its extracellular face to the bath: an outside-out patch.
scenes.visual: Amplifier wired to pipette on a cell, agonist in the pipette, an idealised square-step trace; then two panels: inside-out patch with cytoplasmic face in the bath and outside-out patch with extracellular face in the bath.
scenes.narration: An amplifier holds the pipette at a voltage you choose and records the current that flows. That is voltage clamp. In the cell-attached form, the patch stays on the cell. With an agonist in the pipette, one channel's openings appear as square steps. Pull the patch off with its cytoplasmic face exposed to the bath, and you have an inside-out patch. You can change the solution on that face. Start from whole-cell mode and pull away instead, and the membrane reseals with its extracellular face to the bath: an outside-out patch.

scenes.tts: In whole-cell mode, the pipette gains access to the cell interior, so ions and small molecules exchange between the pipette solution and the cytoplasm. Perforated patch uses a pore-former, gramicidin or nystatin, for electrical access while the cell keeps most of its own contents. In current clamp you set the injected current and record the voltage. A current step gives a voltage response. The steady voltage change, divided by the current, is the input resistance. The charging curve gives the time constant.
scenes.visual: Whole-cell: pipette solution flows into a small cell; perforated patch: pores in the patch, cell contents stay; then a current-clamp plot, idealised: current step above, voltage response below with a steady level and a charging curve.

A current step gives a voltage response. The steady voltage change, divided by the current, is the input resistance. The charging curve gives the time constant.

scenes.tts: The trace sits at zero, steps to a fixed level and steps back as one channel opens and shuts. The step height is the unitary current. The fraction of time the channel is open is the open probability. In this idealised example, the open level is minus two picoamps, open two hundred milliseconds of one second. Open probability is zero point two. After a drug, the level is the same, but the channel is open five hundred milliseconds a second. Open probability is zero point five. The drug changed gating, not conduction.
scenes.visual: An idealised single-channel trace draws in: zero level, step to a fixed level, back; brace for step height; open intervals shaded; second trace after a drug with same level but more open time; example tag on screen.
scenes.caption: The trace sits at zero, steps to a fixed level and steps back as one channel opens and shuts. The step height is the unitary current. The fraction of time the channel is open is the open probability. In this idealised example, the open level is −2 picoamps, open 200 milliseconds of 1 second. Open probability is 0.2. After a drug, the level is the same, but the channel is open 500 milliseconds a second. Open probability is 0.5. The drug changed gating, not conduction.

scenes.tts: Brief closures shorter than the recording can resolve vanish from the trace, so report the filter and the sampling rate. And a conventional whole-cell pipette replaces the cell's chloride, so the gabba reversal potential reflects the experimenter's recipe. Gramicidin perforated patch leaves the cell's chloride alone.
scenes.visual: Left: a trace with brief closures that vanish after filtering, with a note to report filter and sampling rate. Right: whole-cell cell whose chloride is replaced by the pipette's recipe, versus a perforated cell that keeps its own.
scenes.caption: Brief closures shorter than the recording can resolve vanish from the trace, so report the filter and the sampling rate. And a conventional whole-cell pipette replaces the cell's chloride, so the GABA reversal potential reflects the experimenter's recipe. Gramicidin perforated patch leaves the cell's chloride alone.

scenes.tts: Neher and Sakmann recorded single-channel currents from denervated frog muscle in 1976. Their records showed square steps from one channel opening and shutting. In 1981 Hamill, Marty, Neher, Sakmann and Sigworth described the gigaseal methods, including excised patches and whole-cell recording.
scenes.visual: Four rows build one by one: 1976 square steps from one channel in frog muscle, 1981 gigaseal paper, 1991 Nobel Prize, and below, 1970 steps in artificial lipid membranes; each with a source tag.

scenes.tts: In 1985 Rorsman and Trube found that twenty millimolar glucose suppressed potassium channel activity in cell-attached patches of cultured mouse beta cells. Three millimolar A T P on the cytoplasmic face of excised inside-out patches reversibly blocked the channels. The excised patch let them test a metabolite on the inner face. In 1989 Derkach, Surprenant and North recorded serotonin-evoked unitary currents in outside-out patches from guinea-pig enteric neurons. Serotonin opening single channels in patches with no cytoplasm was evidence that the 5-H T 3 receptor is itself a channel. Keep this rule. A current from cultured cells, or from cells engineered to make the channel, belongs to that preparation and protocol, not to a living animal.
scenes.visual: Two panels: an inside-out patch where ATP on the cytoplasmic face closes a potassium channel (Rorsman and Trube 1985), and an outside-out patch where serotonin evokes unitary steps (Derkach, Surprenant and North 1989); then the rule appears in a box.
